hints: Picture a myelinated axon in cross-section - layers of fatty Schwann cell membrane wrapped tightly around it with small gaps at intervals. What effect would that wrapping have on charged particles trying to move in or out?
If ion movement is blocked along most of the axon, think about where voltage-gated sodium and potassium channels must be concentrated to allow depolarisation to still happen.
Recall that depolarisation in one region sets up local currents that depolarise the next region. How would blocking leakage of ions affect how far those currents can reach?
Link the idea of the impulse appearing to jump from gap to gap to the overall speed of transmission, and recall the special name for this.
walkthrough:
Myelin Blocks Ion Flow**
Think of myelin as thick fatty tape wrapped around the axon. Because it is fatty and thick, sodium ions and potassium ions cannot leak or diffuse across the axon membrane where it is covered. In other words, it is an electrical insulator.

Action Potentials Only at the Gaps**
The sheath is not continuous - it leaves tiny exposed gaps called nodes of Ranvier where there are many voltage-gated channels. So depolarisation and regeneration of the action potential can only happen at these nodes, not under the myelin.

Longer Local Currents Mean Jumping and Speed**
When one node depolarises, sodium ions entering set up a local current that spreads inside the axon. Because no ions are lost through the insulated region, that current can travel a long distance to the next node. The action potential therefore appears to jump from node to node. This is saltatory conduction and it makes transmission much faster.

Final answer: Myelin sheath acts as an electrical insulator so ions cannot pass through; depolarisation / action potentials occur only at nodes of Ranvier; this allows longer local circuits / currents; action potential jumps from node to node / saltatory conduction, so transmission is faster.

hints: Start at the very end of the presynaptic neurone - the synaptic knob. What electrical signal must arrive there first to trigger everything that follows?

The presynaptic membrane contains a different type of voltage-gated channel that is sensitive to that electrical change. Which positive ion is much more concentrated outside the neurone in the synaptic cleft?
Once those channels open, think about the transport mechanism that lets that ion rush in - no ATP is needed, so what gradient is it moving down?
Inside the knob there are many tiny membrane sacs filled with acetylcholine. What must those sacs do when the ion concentration inside rises?
Finish the sequence by describing how acetylcholine actually leaves the presynaptic cell and where it goes next.
walkthrough:
Arrival Triggers Calcium Entry**
When the action potential reaches the presynaptic knob, the membrane depolarises. That change in voltage opens voltage-gated $Ca^{2+}$ channels in the presynaptic membrane, greatly increasing its permeability to $Ca^{2+}$.

Calcium Moves Down Its Gradient**
There is a much higher concentration of $Ca^{2+}$ in the synaptic cleft and tissue fluid outside than inside the neurone. So $Ca^{2+}$ rushes into the axoplasm of the knob by facilitated diffusion through the open channels, down its concentration gradient.

Vesicles Fuse and Release ACh**
The rise in $Ca^{2+}$ inside causes synaptic vesicles filled with acetylcholine to move to and fuse with the presynaptic membrane. The vesicle membrane becomes part of the cell membrane and acetylcholine is emptied by exocytosis into the synaptic cleft, ready to diffuse to the postsynaptic membrane.

Final answer: Action potential / depolarisation arrives at presynaptic membrane; $Ca^{2+}$ channels open / increased permeability to $Ca^{2+}$; $Ca^{2+}$ enter presynaptic knob by facilitated diffusion down concentration gradient; vesicles containing acetylcholine fuse with presynaptic membrane; acetylcholine released by exocytosis into synaptic cleft.
